Bring Back the Loot: Repatriating Cultural Heritage

By: Siniketiwe Hlanze | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How do you make right the wrongs of centuries ago, there's a growing global call for European countries to return artifacts looted during colonialism

Unique Selling Point:
Conversations with museum directors, government officials and activist about bringing back artifacts which were taken from colonised countries in Africa and Asia. European are seen to be dragging their feet in create policy that will facilitate the return of some of these artifacts which vary from religious and cultural significance. The piece will also highlight the role that museum, which hold some of these objects, they are able generate profits through these but does it make it morally and ethically correct to continue to hold on to these. Secondly these objects are often sold on private auctions for millions of dollars which never trickles down to the countries of origin.

Summary:
Current coverage on the media focuses primarily on the Benin Bronzes which originate from Nigeria but are kept in museums across Europe and America. The piece will also highlight artifacts from various parts of the continent and their significance. Second to this is the subject of returning remains of bodies which would have been taken by colonial empires as symbols of having conquered smaller African kingdoms. Oxford professor Dan Hicks and author of The Brutush Museum writes in his book some of these are kept in private collections.

Further information:
French ambassador Aurélien Lechevallier, will talk about the previously returned artifacts to West African nations and the newly conceptualised legislation that will see more of these being repatriated.

Prof Dan Hicks, will talk about the research he has done into the British Museum and the haul of objects that they hold and the feeble policy to engage countries that have asked for their artifacts to be returned.

Onyakechi Wambu - Founder of AFFORD an organisation that works with the diaspora community to improve lives on the African continent is now channelling its efforts to force museums to release these artifacts. The organisation has come up with policy which can guide both governments and museums on how to facilitate the return of these object.

Léontine Meijer-van Mensch, director of Dresden Museum in collaboration with Artist Emeka Ogboh have created a campaign for Germany to return the objects they have in their museum. Highlighting that will that some European Museum may have to release these but there's no political will from the state to return them.

Emeka Ogboh - Artist, will speak about the posters he has created and the meaning behind them to raise awareness on about the Bronzes.

Ines de Castro - Director of the Linden Museum in Germany, which returned artifacts to Namibia in 2019, will talk about the complex process that they followed. in this instance they could trace the original family that owned the objects however these had now become state heritage property.

Extra Budget Items:
Many of the interviews will be conducted online and therefore need visually interesting location to shoot them from. One particular gallery has asked for a R2500 fee to accommodate us.

Script:


The punitive wars staged by colonial powers against nations and kingdoms were vicious.
And as reward for their triumph, soldiers and military officials would take what was left behind.

Looted from the Benin Kingdom, present day southern Nigeria were cultural relics, symbolic items and royal artifacts..

These stories of colonial conquest in the 1800s are common across africa
Thousands of these artifacts, from the continent, south America and Asia are now prized positions in western museums.
LINK
Museums are facing a moment of reckoning...


Dr Friedriech Von Bose is the head of research and exhibitions at the Dresden State Museum, in Saxony Germany.
27;33 Friedrich –

They have been in our storages for more than a hundred years.
The Benin bronzes are elaborate sculptures that vary from caricatures of sacred animals, members of the palace and items that held meaning for the kingdom.
18:22 Friedrich –
For Dresden, they were bought on the art market from like around 1900s.
Through a collaborative effort with artist, Emeka Ogboh, they started a campaign of missing poster, to get the attention of federal government authorities to start the process of returning these artifacts.
Claire: 14:31
So take us through the process then of returning these bronzes, why couldn’t you just package them and send them
14:47 Freidrich

It’s the state of Saxony which officially owns the objects, that we officially administer you could say. We are, as a museum, we do the provenance research, we care for the collections, we display them in the galleries, but ultimately they don’t belong to the museum. And that’s why we need the politics on board to make the decision, to make the call.
19;27 ines
In the linden museum, we don’t only deal with restitutions for artifacts for African countries. We are in talks for example with societies in Australia but also with Afghanistan, for looted stone objects for example.
Ines de castro is the director of the linden museum in stuttgart, germany.

After consultations between officials in her country and Namibia, her museum returned a bible and a whip confiscated from Captain Hendrik Witbooi, chief of the Nama, who led an insurrection against German colonial occupation.
06;24 Ines:
According to our archives, they were probably looted in 1893 and then these two objects, we don’t know how and in what way but they came to the linden museum in 1902.
After namibia had made a formal request for these items - the german government took a decision for these to be returned in February 2019.




Hage Geingob
00:33 If we are to move forward then it is important for the german government to admit, as you did, the wrongs committed against the people of namibia


De Castro says, the museum’s role in this process is to endorse or support the submission by former colonies


Ines
11;02 And then quite quickly the acquisition of the objects is checked, the value of the objects is checked, in a symbolic way also. It makes a big difference if you can say these objects are important symbolically for countries or society. Or if the acquisition context was very critical, if they were looted in a attack or military position then there is a good chance really to get support and start dialogue on a possible restitution
De castro and von bose are some of few maverick voices in the musem world. Many of these institutions worry that once they start engaging in restitutions, they will be left with nothing to display.
15;25 ines
I don’t share with some of my colleagues, this idea that the museums will get empty.
The restitutions, in most cases, they are related to only a couple of objects. For sure it is important for us that some of the objects stay in our museum also, to tell the story because we have this entangled history with Namibia
LINK
Manuscripts, artwork and sculptures, the things that are symbols of a people’s heritage are still in vaults in musems, far from the places of origin. Is there political will for these to be repatriated.

French ambassador 12;07 it was a taboo for a long time, people would say these art collections are untouchable, so we can not do it
In December last year, france enacted a new legislation which would see the restitution of large scale artifacts to some of its former colonies.


Ambassador Aurélien Lechevallier says the new policy will expedite the return of these items, including a crown which belonged Madagascar’s last reigning queen



Madagascar crown return



14;03
now we have started this restitution process with Madagascar. We have also very important, symbolic art from Senegal that was given to the people in Dakar last year, the sword of El Hajj Umar Tall, and now we are starting the process to also restitutte 26 art pieces to Benin.
11;13 French Ambassador
90% of the African heritage is outside Africa and it’s very important for the African public especially the young generation, that they can have access to this African heritage.
Onyekachi
38:55 we want Africans to discuss what do these icons mean to us in the present time, so this project is really about africans and once we understand what it means to us, we will demand it with the passion that we should
Onyekachi wambu is the founder of AFFORD - a UK based organisation - which is calling for these artifacts to be returned and creates policy guidelines for states and stakeholders
Onyekachi
16:45 The Germans have said that they want to return everything, not just cultural icons, human remains but they’re even talking about returning natural stuff, so skeletons, dinosaurs.
18;06
The British are, government is very ambiguous at the moment and you know the mood music is they don't want to return this. There’s some stakeholders who feel that they should go back and return the material.
24:38 Claire question

25:03 Well that’s a difficult question, because obviously when the art piece falls under the public domain, then you know and we know how to do it. We have to pass a law, we need this policy framework that we were talking about but when an art piece belongs to a private owner, this is difficult. We need advocacy, we need more awareness, we need to incentivise.
Onyekachi
30:31
It’s an elephant and you have to eat it slowly, you know, so we’re starting with the ones that are in national and public collections.
It would take years before a comprehensive inventory of these artifacts is created.

and in some instances countries simply don’t know that they may have symbolic relics in museums - De Castro says more transparency can bring a resolution to the restitution conversation
26;05 ines –
We do it also in a very proactive way, sometimes countries don’t come to us. We openly go towards these countries to say, here listen these are the objects we have from your society are you interested in starting a dialogue process.



Promos:
Academics, activists and artists in former colonies, around the world, are demanding the return of looted cultural artifacts from western museums - will these institutions comply



After decades of campaigns to return symbolic artifacts looted in the colonial era, states in the west are slowly starting the process of repatriation

As the demand for looted cultural items to be returned from europe to African countries, many western museums claim they will be left with nothing to display

metadata.Further information: French ambassador Aurélien Lechevallier, will talk about the previously returned artifacts to West African nations and the newly conceptualised legislation that will see more of these being repatriated. Prof Dan Hicks, will talk about the research he has done into the British Museum and the haul of objects that they hold and the feeble policy to engage countries that have asked for their artifacts to be returned. Onyakechi Wambu - Founder of AFFORD an organisation that works with the diaspora community to improve lives on the African continent is now channelling its efforts to force museums to release these artifacts. The organisation has come up with policy which can guide both governments and museums on how to facilitate the return of these object. Léontine Meijer-van Mensch, director of Dresden Museum in collaboration with Artist Emeka Ogboh have created a campaign for Germany to return the objects they have in their museum. Highlighting that will that some European Museum may have to release these but there's no political will from the state to return them. Emeka Ogboh - Artist, will speak about the posters he has created and the meaning behind them to raise awareness on about the Bronzes. Ines de Castro - Director of the Linden Museum in Germany, which returned artifacts to Namibia in 2019, will talk about the complex process that they followed. in this instance they could trace the original family that owned the objects however these had now become state heritage property.
